To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the 5' (50 kb) and 3' (20 kb) flanking regions of a human globin locus, containing DNAase I hypersensitive sites, are sufficient for position independent expression in mice, that this expression is tissue-specific (erythroid), and that the expression is as high per gene copy as that of the mouse beta-globn gene.
the human beta-globein minilocus is transcribed tissue-specifically in the erythroid lineage of transgenic mice and that the expression of this minilocus is position-independent and high-level.

the 5' flanking region of the human beta globin gene contains a dominant regulatory sequence that specifies position independent and tissue specific expression of the gene and that this sequence is normally active in the human beta glob in locus.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development and application of transgenic mice for the study of gene structure and function.
the molecular basis of tissue-specific expression.
the molecular biology of the human beta globin gene and its expression in transgenic mice and in erythroid cell lines.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the human beta-gloin minilocus, when placed in the transgenic mouse, is capable of being expressed in a tissue-specific and copy-number dependent manner, but independent of its position in the genome.
the beta-globins are the most important and important aspects of the human beta globin gene.
this minilocus has all of the properties of a complete locus and is a model of the endogenous human beta-globins locus.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the 3' flanks of the beta-globein locus are not necessary for position-independent, high-level gene expression.
the human beta-gloin gene is expressed position-independent in transgenic mice and that the expression is regulated at the same level in all the transgenic mice.

the 3.5 kb of DNA flanking the human β-gene is sufficient to confer position-independent, tissue-specific expression in transgenic mice, and that this region contains a dominant regulatory element that can be separated from the enhancer element by 10 kb of DNA.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the human beta-gloin locus can be expressed in transgenic mice in a position-independent manner, and this expression can be controlled by the human beta-globein promoter.
the human beta-globein locus is expressed at a level directly proportional to its copy number and independent of its position within the genome.
the beta-globins locus control region is capable of directing high-level expression in transgenic mice and that it is capable of directing position-independent expression.
